The rise of AI has led to an explosive growth in small companies and startups, each of which likely will need some commonly used software that they won’t want to write.

At this point, I’d rather bet on good incumbent software companies to adopt AI efficiently to improve their products and further entrench their leadership.

First, bringing up “Plaza Accord” in any such discussion is sure to backfire. The folk legend in China is that the US jealous of Japan’s economic growth used the accord as a means to force the vassal state to sharply appreciate the JPY and led to/exacerbated Japan’s economic decline and orchestrated the “lost decades”. Plenty in China are already convinced that that’s the US’s plan for China again.

Ofc it’s far from clear that the Accord really has its intended effect and not something that was put in way too late as a political maneuver when the window for addressing the economic problem had long passed. 

More generally, I’m not sure what’s exactly being proposed here. Chinese exports are already subject to tariffs. Chinese cars are subject to so much tariffs and other restrictions that you don’t see them on American streets at all. In fact, successive Trump admin fought two major global trade wars with the tariffs on Chinese imports at the heart of it all. 

Nevertheless, here we are. Chinese exports are still surging albeit less to the US and CNY still undervalued allegedly. The US is still engaged in trade talks with China with plenty of give and takes. Clearly, the tariff threats haven’t really worked. The US doesn’t have such dominant economic leverage over China: it needs key input factors from China like rare earth minerals and also needs the cheap consumer goods from China to offset domestic services inflation. 

Suppose the US really managed to get Chinese imports to become 35% more expensive, are there realistic alternative sources of production to help mitigate the net price increases? Bc the consumers for sure don’t want to pay 35% more for economic security or protection of domestic producers. And if the price differential isn’t fully erased, do Chinese exporters win out anyway bc of sheer production efficiency due to supply chain completeness?

It’s not obvious to me that the application of the so called “law of one price” is really appropriate here. LOOP states that the same thing should cost the same everywhere minus transportation costs. It doesn’t require that all producers have the same cost structure, productivity and comparative advantages. A t shirt made in a poor developing country will always be cheaper than one made in lower Manhattan bc of differences in cost of labor. China has further advantages in automation. 

I think this whole discussion merits an upgrade. It’s 2026. Surely the answer has to be more than just “China manipulates its currency and the CNY is undervalued!”?

I’m always on the lookout for high-quality, low-maintenance yield.

And after all the exploits and protocol shutdowns in 2026, I became even pickier about where I park my stables.

Some DeFi yield setups are closer to my preference, though, like the one from @Mantle_Official's Grove vault. Btw, the same vault was previously available on Bybit, and now it's also onchain.

I personally prefer farming onchain yield either way.

This one in particular is non-custodial, doesn’t use leverage, and the rewards come from separate sources.

Let me guide you through the process ↓

1/ Deposit USDC

• Go to @Fluxion_network's platform
• Open the "Earn" tab
• Choose the Mantle USDC Grove Yield Layer vault
• Deposit a USDC amount higher than $500

There’s nothing else to manage after that. @CIAN_protocol handles the underlying strategy inside the vault.

2/ Track the yield

Once deposited, your position appears directly on Fluxion.

There are three separate components:

• Native yield from Sky Savings (~3.5%)
• Up to ~6.5% APR in @grovedotfinance incentives
• @Fluxion_network points

The native yield shows through the vault’s share price, which updates every three days. So your balance won’t visibly increase every block as it does in some other DeFi products.

3/ Claim GROVE rewards

GROVE incentives are separate from the native Sky yield.

You can check and claim them through Merkl directly from the Fluxion interface (the "Rewards" tab), while Fluxion points accrue separately.

The main thing here is I can track the sustainable yield and the temporary incentives separately. I actually prefer this structure.

4/ Withdraw

If you want to exit the strategy, you can submit a withdrawal request from the same interface.

Grove processes withdrawals from the underlying strategy within roughly 3-5 days, and you can only have one request per asset active at a time.

5/ Conclusion

For me, the main difference to other yield products is the maintenance burden. I don’t need to monitor borrow rates, health factors, or expiries like I would with more active DeFi strategies.

Compared with looping on @Morpho or managing PT/YT positions on @pendle_fi, this requires far less maintenance.

I already have so much to keep track of. I don’t need my stablecoin yield to become another unnecessary hassle.

At this point, I’m optimizing for peace of mind as much as APY.

For the record, I'm a long-term $MNT holder and Mantle supporter, just couldn't ignore a yield opportunity so juicy.

Happy Monday, my friends.

My week started with a report from Bessemer Venture Partners on their framework for evaluating AI services (highly recommended).

There’s a very interesting infographic showing how they rated eight major service markets against their 11-criterion scorecard.

In short:

01–02: Is the market fragmented (many small players), and are the incumbents capable of fending off AI newcomers?

03–04: Are errors critical, and will the market grow in volume if AI lowers the service price (the Jevons Paradox)?

05–06: Is there a labor shortage, and what share of the cost does human labor account for?

07–08: Is AI performance easy to verify, and does the monetization model allow the company to capture the margin?

09–10: Is there a subscription model (recurring revenue), and is a “data flywheel” forming as the AI gets smarter with each client?

11: Does government regulation help or hinder?

Based on the answers, we have these service centric rankings. Two principles:

> The bigger and rounder the shape, the more uniformly attractive and investable the market is for an AI-native startup.

> Deep spikes inward represent fatal flaws. As Bessemer flags, a sharp dent indicates specific criteria that could completely sink an investment.

So, what are we building, guys?

PS: Report link: https://t.co/JMWnTXyVN6

Happy Monday, my friends.

My week started with a report from Bessemer Venture Partners on their framework for evaluating AI services (highly recommended).

There’s a very interesting infographic showing how they rated eight major service markets against their 11-criterion scorecard.

In short:

01–02: Is the market fragmented (many small players), and are the incumbents capable of fending off AI newcomers?

03–04: Are errors critical, and will the market grow in volume if AI lowers the service price (the Jevons Paradox)?

05–06: Is there a labor shortage, and what share of the cost does human labor account for?

07–08: Is AI performance easy to verify, and does the monetization model allow the company to capture the margin?

09–10: Is there a subscription model (recurring revenue), and is a “data flywheel” forming as the AI gets smarter with each client?

11: Does government regulation help or hinder?

Based on the answers, we have these service centric rankings. Two principles:

> The bigger and rounder the shape, the more uniformly attractive and investable the market is for an AI-native startup.

> Deep spikes inward represent fatal flaws. As Bessemer flags, a sharp dent indicates specific criteria that could completely sink an investment.

🇯🇵 Takaichi has just requested nearly ¥9 trillion for defense spending in 2027. Another sign that Tokyo is entering a new fiscal regime at exactly the wrong time as its debt is finally becoming expensive to carry.

📊 The headline amount is probably only a starting point as around 160 items remain uncosted ahead of the defense plan review due by year-end. Japan wants to accelerate spending on long-range missiles, drones, AI, maritime surveillance and stand-off strike capabilities. As nominal GDP has risen significantly, simply maintaining defense spending at 2% of GDP now means roughly ¥13.8tn a year, versus around ¥11tn previously. If Japan were ever to move closer to the 3.5% level Washington is pushing allies toward, we would be talking about roughly ¥24tn a year.

📈 Obviously, the problem is that Japan is no longer financing all of this in a zero-rate world. Debt-service costs for 2027 are expected to rise toward ¥36.6tn while interest expenses are climbing rapidly. Moreover, every bond that matures is gradually being refinanced at much higher rates. Japan’s average debt maturity, at roughly 9 to 10 years, still protects it from a sudden shock but it also means the increase in interest costs will slowly feed through for years. Meanwhile, Takaichi is stacking up spending commitments in defense, industrial policy, growth support, strategic investment, a temporary consumption-tax cut on food, all without fully closing the fiscal equation.

🤷‍♂️ Then, the BOJ’s dilemma gets even more important. If it tightens enough to support the yen and contain inflation, it puts more pressure on JGBs and debt-service costs. On the other hand, if it protects the bond market too aggressively, it risks renewed yen weakness. It is clear that the tension between monetary policy and fiscal policy is becoming much harder to ignore.

Japan is changing regime before the bond market begins imposing its own limits.

Lots of bear posts on the timeline, which is to be expected as there is still an ongoing battle between those who believe we’ve had a trend shift and those who believe we still have our low to come. 

From a technical point of view we don’t have strict confirmation. 

But, I am still in the bulls camp.

A lot of those in the bear camp point to the 4 year cycle, without understanding cycle theory. 

There is room either side of the 4 year mark for a cycle bottom. This is perfectly fine, so isn’t a reason to remain a bear and on the sidelines by itself, which is where I think there is confusion. 

Perfectly trusting exact historical patterns (exact bottom of 12 months of bear) doesn’t overwhelm market context for me. I would even call Bessent’s intervention a kind of white swan, which forced an impulse to set up a slightly earlier 4 year cycle low. 

For me as a bull, invalidation and new macro low would be caused by some sort of cataclysmic drop in the stock market, some macro crisis, or some horrible new event unique to Bitcoin which is unforeseeable. 

82k is the final level which bears have to hold onto, or they are extinct for another cycle.

I think we will still have to endure another drop where everyone questions everything. 200D MA will likely get tested, and everyone that said they wanted to buy the dip won’t actually buy because they will believe in lower prices once we are down there.

Allocating before you have confirmation of a trend shift has always paid very well historically, because you are taking on the risk of being underwater/wrong, and when we finally turn you are set up strongly. 

Obviously doing this too early is a bad idea, but we were in the timing band for a low, so R/R was very much in the favour of long term buyers. 

If you don’t have conviction in this asset class, or the specific high quality assets we have in crypto (not many) then I understand why you don’t want to buy/hold without confirmation.

One thing has always remained true across all cycles is holders of the best assets in crypto who ride the volatility from despair/denial to euphoria make incredible returns. 

It takes actual conviction to do this.

This time won’t be different. 

We have a long way to go.

Over the weekend I watched an interview with David Einhorn, who is undoubtedly far more intelligent than I am.

He explained that performance had been poor over the last couple of years because the type of investing they do simply hasn’t been working.

It is very interesting to watch how many great investors struggle to adapt when the market changes.

What worked for ten years becomes part of who they are, and changing it feels almost like admitting they were wrong.

But markets change.

And if you cannot change with them, eventually your old edge becomes your biggest weakness.

And to me, that is the entire lesson.

Markets do not reward you for being loyal to a strategy.

They reward you for adapting.

Last year I told the story of my favorite client, Oscar.

In 2022, when the market was down around 20%, Oscar was up around 20%. A big reason was the way I used the $VIX.

If you look at the comments below that story, someone told me that you cannot compare Oscar’s performance with someone who doesn’t know how to use the $VIX.

But we are in the business of making money.

How can you afford to know only one way to make money?

Only know how to be long stocks.
Only know value investing.
Only know technical analysis.
Only know momentum.
Only know volatility.

A strategy is just a tool.

The goal is not to prove that your favorite tool works.

The goal is to make money.

Around the same period, I was also consulting for a hedge fund that had started operating in 2021.

Luckily for the fund manager, the environment at the time was almost perfectly suited to the strategy we were using. We were using primarily VIX-related trades, and between 2021 and 2022 the returns looked extraordinary.

The fund was still small because it had just started, but on a percentage basis it was outperforming its peers by a very large margin.

By the time the market was down around 20%, the fund was still up around 10%.

That was exactly when I believed the opportunity had shifted.

Equities had become significantly more attractive, while the $VIX trades that had worked so well for us were becoming increasingly dangerous.

I told the hedge fund manager it was time to change. Reduce the volatility trades and start buying stocks.

He had no interest in buying equities.

His reasoning was simple: the $VIX trades had worked incredibly well. Why stop doing what was working?

But that is exactly the trap.

I disagreed strongly enough that I issued a formal letter. Always put things in writing, even with friends. When people look back at the past, they have a convenient habit of forgetting exactly how things happened and avoiding responsibility for the decisions they made. In the letter, I explained the risks I saw in continuing with those volatility trades and why I believed the volatility landscape had changed.

He decided to continue anyway.
The following months were catastrophic.

Meanwhile, Oscar and the portfolios I directly managed rotated into stocks and were up substantially.

There is no strategy that deserves your loyalty.

Sometimes the right tool is VIX.
Sometimes it is equities.
Sometimes it is value.
Sometimes it is momentum.
Sometimes it is cash.

Your job is not to become emotionally attached to what made you money yesterday.

Your job is to recognize what environment you are in today.

It is not necessarily the smartest that survives.

It is the one that adapts.

Markets are not much different.

Your edge is not VIX.
Your edge is not value investing.
Your edge is not understanding tech.
Your edge is not mastering macro.

Your edge is being able to change when the market changes.
